Succourer
SUK-ur-ur
n. (one who runs to help another in distress; Paul's word for Phebe)
From Latin succurrere, to run beneath or run to help — sub-, under, and currere, to run. The help is not sent from a distance; the succourer goes under the load. It renders Greek prostatis, a patroness or one who stands before another.

Biblical Definition

Paul closes Romans by commending Phebe, a servant of the church at Cenchrea, and asks the Romans to receive her and assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of, for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also. The Greek prostatis means one who stands before another to help — a patroness, a protector, one who puts her own standing and resources between a needy person and their need. Paul, who could say he had learned in whatsoever state he was therewith to be content, says plainly that this woman had helped him. The Latin behind our English word says it even better: to succour is to run underneath, to get beneath a weight someone else is failing to carry. That is why the word belongs supremely to Christ: in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted. He is qualified to run underneath our load because he has carried it. And God speaks of himself the same way through Isaiah, quoted by Paul: in the day of salvation have I succoured thee. The order runs from God to the church and out through people like Phebe — helped, so helping; run to, so running.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one that affords relief; a helper; one that runs to the aid of another in difficulty or distress.

expand to see more

SUCCOURER, n. He that affords relief; a helper; a deliverer.

SUCCOUR, v.t. To run to, or run to support; hence, to help or relieve when in difficulty, want or distress.

RELIEVE, v.t. To free, wholly or partially, from pain, grief, want, anxiety or distress.

PATRONESS, n. A female that favors or supports; a woman that protects or countenances.

ASSIST, v.t. To help; to aid; to succor; to give support to in some undertaking.

Key Scripture

Romans 16:2 — "That ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also."

Hebrews 2:18 — "For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted."

2 Corinthians 6:2 — "(For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.)"

Psalm 46:1 — "To the chief Musician for the sons of Korah, A Song upon Alamoth. God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble."

Modern Corruption

Phebe is enlisted as a proof text in the argument over the pastoral office, which loses the woman entirely; Paul commends her for what she did — she stood between many believers and their need, including him.

expand to see more

Romans 16:1-2 has been fought over so long that Phebe herself has nearly disappeared behind the argument. One side presses diakonos and prostatis into an office of rule; the other, wary of the move, hurries past her in two sentences. Both lose what Paul actually wrote. He names her, commends her to a church that had never met her, asks that she be received in the Lord as becometh saints, asks that they assist her in whatsoever business she has, and gives the reason: she has been a succourer of many, and of Paul. That is a substantial, costly, publicly acknowledged ministry, and the apostle who elsewhere orders the offices of the church is the one honouring it.

The honest reading holds both. Scripture reserves the office of elder to qualified men, and Scripture fills its pages with women whose labour the church could not have done without — the women who ministered to Christ of their substance, Priscilla who expounded the way of God more perfectly to Apollos, Lydia whose house received the first church in Europe, Phebe carrying a letter to Rome. A church that uses the New Testament's order as a reason to leave such women unnamed and unassisted has not obeyed the New Testament. Paul's instruction about Phebe is a command with a practical object: receive her, and help her.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek prostatis (G4368), a patroness, one who stands before; boetheo (G997), to run to the aid of a cry; diakonos (G1249), a servant; Hebrew azar (H5826), to help.

expand to see more

Greek prostatis (G4368) — one who stands before another as protector; used once, of Phebe.

Greek boetheo (G997) — to run at a cry for help; the verb rendered succour in Hebrews 2 and in the Syrophenician's Lord, help me.

Greek diakonos (G1249) — a servant or minister; Paul's word for Phebe's relation to the church at Cenchrea.

Hebrew azar (H5826) — to help, to surround with aid; the root of Ebenezer, the stone of help.

Latin succurrere — to run underneath; the picture our English word preserves better than the Greek.

Usage

"“she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also” — an apostle admitting he was helped."

"“he is able to succour them that are tempted” — qualified by having carried it."

"“in the day of salvation have I succoured thee” — God running underneath first."
